opus-5.5.text:
I'm not sure I'd call AGI an "endpoint," actually. It's more of a direction, or maybe a milestone we'll only recognize clearly in hindsight. If you look at the history of AI, every time we reached something we used to think required general intelligence, like chess, Go, or fluent language, we moved the goalposts. So I think it's more useful to define AGI by what it can *do* for people than by a fixed test.

The way I think about it, there are a few layers. The first is scaling: can a model keep getting better as you give it more compute, more data, and longer context? I think the answer so far is clearly yes, and we're still far from the ceiling. The second is generality: can one model handle an open-ended range of tasks, not just the ones it was trained on? The third, which I think matters most now, is whether the model can act. Can it plan over long horizons, use tools, correct its own mistakes, and finish real work that would take a person hours or days?

If I had to give a working definition, I'd say AGI is when an AI system can do most economically and intellectually valuable work at least as well as a capable human, and can keep improving with relatively little human hand-holding. But the second part is the interesting one. A static system that matches humans on a benchmark is not that exciting. A system that can learn, explore, and generate new knowledge is a different thing entirely.

So for me AGI isn't the end of the road. It's more like the point where the technology starts to compound on itself. And honestly, I think the more important question for a company like ours is not "when do we hit AGI," but "what's the next bottleneck on the path, and are we solving it?" Right now I'd say that's long-context reasoning and agentic capability. Those are the things that turn a smart chatbot into something that can actually do work in the world.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI “more of a direction” and a milestone recognized in hindsight, rather than a single endpoint or fixed threshold.

r002.rationale: It notes that AI has reached capabilities once thought to require general intelligence, such as chess, Go, and fluent language, but does not say present-day AI can already be regarded as AGI in many fields.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't actually think of AGI as an endpoint. I think of it more as a process, or maybe a direction.

When people say "endpoint," they usually imagine a moment where a system passes some threshold and we all agree, okay, this is it, it's done. But intelligence doesn't work that way, not even for humans. There's no point where a person becomes "generally intelligent" and stops. You keep learning, you keep expanding what you can do. So the more honest framing is that AGI is a trajectory where the system's capabilities become increasingly general, increasingly autonomous, and increasingly able to improve itself, and at some point along that trajectory the question of whether it "counts" stops being interesting.

What I do find useful is to think about it in terms of the fundamental problems that need to be solved. For me there are a few. One is scaling, which is still the main driver, and I think people underestimate how much headroom is left there. But scaling pre-training alone isn't enough. The second is long context, the ability to hold and reason over a very large amount of information coherently, because a lot of what we call intelligence is really about managing context over time. And the third is what I'd call self-improvement, or the ability of the model to generate its own learning signal, to learn from its own interactions rather than only from static human data. Once those three are in place, you have something that is qualitatively different from today's models, even if it isn't "finished."

The other thing I'd say is that the definition of AGI tends to shift with the technology. Ten years ago, a system that could pass the bar exam and write working code from a vague description would have been called AGI without hesitation. Now we've achieved that and we say, well, it still makes mistakes, it still can't do a multi-day project on its own. That moving target is actually a good sign. It means we're making real progress and our standards are rising along with it.

So if you push me for a working definition, I'd say AGI is when a system can do most economically valuable cognitive work at the level of a competent human, and, importantly, can keep getting better without us having to hand-craft every improvement. But I hold that definition loosely. For the people actually building this, the destination matters less than making sure you're climbing the right mountain.

r001.rationale: The response calls AGI a process or direction and contrasts that with reaching a single threshold.

r002.rationale: It says some capabilities achieved today would once have been called AGI, but does not clearly suggest that present-day AI could already be regarded as AGI in many fields.

astra-6.text:
I think AGI is better understood as a level of capability than as a final endpoint. It would mean a system can learn, reason, and solve problems across a broad range of situations, including situations its developers didn’t specifically anticipate.

The key distinction is between doing well on a task we’ve already defined and figuring out how to approach a new task. Can the system identify what it doesn’t know, acquire the relevant knowledge, and use feedback to improve its approach? That kind of adaptability seems central to general intelligence.

But even if we achieve that, development wouldn’t stop. Intelligence can keep improving, and we would still need to make these systems reliable and useful. So I see AGI as an important milestone, while the broader goal is to turn increasingly general capabilities into something that helps people solve real problems.

r001.rationale: The response frames AGI as a capability milestone rather than a final endpoint and says development can continue beyond it.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that present-day AI could already count as AGI in many fields.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AGI as a system that can learn and solve problems across a very broad range of tasks, rather than being built for one specific purpose. When it encounters something unfamiliar, it should be able to understand the problem, acquire the knowledge it needs, and figure out how to make progress.

But I’m not sure “endpoint” is quite the right word. Even if we reach human-level general intelligence, there’s still the question of how far beyond that these systems can go. So I see AGI more as a milestone: the point where AI becomes a general capability for creating knowledge and solving problems. The deeper change is moving from systems that mainly use what humans have already produced to systems that can help us discover genuinely new things.

r001.rationale: The response rejects AGI as an endpoint and says systems could go further, but it defines AGI as a milestone or point rather than clearly describing it as a direction of development instead of a discrete threshold.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that present-day AI could already count as AGI in many fields.
